text.p: Superdrug, the British toiletries retailer, launched its own "corporate smell" at its flagship London store on Tuesday to get customers in the mood for shopping.
The chocolate aroma is pumped around the store via the air conditioning system.
A Superdrug spokeswoman said, "We have undergone a major refurbishment programme and this is designed to enhance the whole shopping experience and give Superdrug a sense of fun."
Industry analysts say they expect retail groups, which are fighting for market share, to turn increasingly to tactics like interesting smells in order to lure shoppers.
The heady cocoa smell launched at the Superdrug store on Tuesday was developed by BOC Gases, Britain's largest industrial gas supplier.
"We make no claims that it will make people shop more but it does improve the shopping environment," Business development manager Chris McGolpin told Reuters.
"People's sense of smell is very powerful and smells remain in the memory. If stores can pump out music, why not aromas?" he said.
One shopper was ambivalent to the new smell.
"It's quite strong and chocolatey. It's a bit overwhelming," she told Reuters.
Superdrug has already tried musk and "baby" smells in 20 of its stores and is planning to roll them out to a further 30 outlets by the end of the year.

The chocolate smell has been launched to coincide with Valentine's Day (February 14) and Superdrug's spokeswoman said it may consider using other smells for short periods of time to celebrate other holidays or to reflect in-store promotions.
McGolpin said that BOC gases was currently talking to a number of other retailers as well as banks, hotels, night-clubs and car manufacturers about developing more corporate smells.
At Christmas it created a "Christmas smell" -- a mixture of pumpkin and thyme -- for Woolworths, the retail chain.
Implementing a corporate smell is relatively cheap, said McGolpin. It costs about 1,500 pounds ($2,450) to install and up to 350 pounds to run for a year.
Given that it is fairly inexpensive to create, industry observers believe that shoppers are likely to experience a lot more of them in the future.
"Smell can be a very powerful part of branding," Irene Inskip, a director at branding consultancy CLK said.

"Retailing is increasingly about becoming a total experience and I think most shoppers would prefer a fresh ozone smell than a slightly sweaty odour in a bank or shoe shop, for example," she told Reuters.

Andy Milligan, brand identity director for branding specialists Interbrand said, "Companies are increasingly recognising the importance of smell and some are starting to register smells as trademarks. It's a very serious business.
"Pirelli has already registered the smell of its tyres because they believe it is very distinctive and goes towards making a Pirelli tyre, a Pirelli tyre," he said.
